[PAPER_0048, relevance_score=0.390] In utilizing EMA, we sought to capture a naturalistic assessment of these social, emotional, and behavioral experiences. All hypotheses are listed in Table 1.

First, we investigated the effects of daily capitalization on the capitalizer's momentary feelings of gratitude. Because capitalization draws the capitalizer's attention to their good fortune in life and has a myriad of benefits, we propose engagement in capitalization and more frequent capitalization predict higher daily gratitude (Hypothesis 1a [H1a]).

[PAPER_0049, relevance_score=0.274] Based on the aging literature and work on social closeness, older adults may benefit more emotionally from capitalization than younger adults, and closeness with the responder may foster more emotional benefits for the capitalizer. Accordingly, we hypothesized that age (Hypothesis 1b [H1b]) and closeness (in the moment and on average; Hypothesis 1c [H1c]) strengthen the associations between capitalization and gratitude.

Second, we sought to examine how trait active-constructive PRCA relates to the capitalizer's feelings of gratitude.

[PAPER_0050, relevance_score=0.271] Perceptions of the responses a capitalizer receives help determine the emotional outcomes of disclosing positive events with another person. Thus, we propose that holding the belief that one's interaction partners characteristically respond enthusiastically to their relayed positive events is associated with higher daily gratitude (Hypothesis 2a [H2a]). Assessing potential moderators, we expect age (Hypothesis 2b [H2b]) and closeness (in the moment and on average; Hypothesis 2c [H2c]) amplify the association between trait active-constructive PRCA and gratitude.

[PAPER_0051, relevance_score=0.318] Third, we assessed the effect of trait active-constructive PRCA on future capitalization attempts. We propose that to continue reaping the benefits of capitalization, people who believe their interaction partners characteristically respond enthusiastically to their capitalization attempts will engage in capitalization more often (Hypothesis 3a [H3a]).

[PAPER_0052, relevance_score=0.360] Like before, we expect age (Hypothesis 3b [H3b]) and closeness (in the moment and on average; Hypothesis 3c [H3c]) to strengthen the association between active-constructive PRCA and capitalization frequency.1

[PAPER_0053, relevance_score=0.361] Method

Transparency and Openness

This study's sample size, which included variables, hypotheses, and planned analyses, was preregistered on Open Science Framework in two separate registrations separated by the independent variable: daily capitalization (https://osf.io/3hdcz/) and active-constructive PRCA (https://osf.io/r9k4s/).

[PAPER_0077, relevance_score=0.366] We ran secondary analyses to test the preregistered hypothesis examining the association between capitalization and closeness to replicate previous work. Controlling for age, people felt higher closeness on occasions where they capitalized compared to those where they did not capitalize. We further conducted exploratory analyses assessing lagged effects of gratitude. Controlling for gratitude at the previous prompt, all effects reported below hold in these models. Detailed results for these secondary and exploratory analyses are reported in Secondary Analysis, Exploratory Analysis, and Tables S5-S9 in the online supplemental materials .

[PAPER_0117, relevance_score=0.390] We also provide some initial evidence of the iterative nature of capitalization through linking regular perceived active-constructive responses with capitalization attempts in daily life contexts.

1

An additional, preregistered hypothesis (Hypothesis 4 [H4]; Table 1) replicates prior work assessing the association between capitalization and closeness.

[PAPER_0055, relevance_score=0.491] Participants

The sample included 290 participants aged 25-85 years old (M = 53.11, SD = 17.06) from a community within the Midwest. Participants were recruited to participate in a larger study on the role of social relationships and cognitive resources in emotion regulation across the adult lifespan. The sample size was established through considerations for that larger study. Of all the participants, 61.4% were women, 37.9% men, and 0.7% other gender.

[PAPER_0058, relevance_score=0.288] Marital status was broken down as 47.9% married, 22.8% single, 16.2% in a committed relationship, 9.3% divorced or separated, 2.4% widowed, and 1.4% did not provide this information. Participants could read and speak English in their homes and had normal cognitive functioning, as determined by scoring below 2 on the self-report Ascertain-Dementia (adapted from Galvin et al., 2005). The Washington University in St. Louis Institutional Review Board approved this study.

[PAPER_0068, relevance_score=0.418] Procedure

The original format of the protocol involved two in-lab sessions with a period of EMA between them. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, there was an alternate protocol for a subset of participants (N = 79) in which they completed trait measures at home and then engaged in the EMA portion of the study. Under this alternate protocol, participants were consented and provided the EMA tutorial over the phone with an experimenter before completing the EMA portion of the study.

[PAPER_0069, relevance_score=0.338] During the first in-lab visit, participants completed a trait-level survey that included measures of capitalization and physical health, among various other measures unrelated to the current research, and were then guided through a tutorial for the EMA component of the study with an experimenter. Participants were reminded they would receive the same survey six times per day during their preferred 12-hr window for 10 consecutive days through an app on their smartphone. The experimenter explained each survey question that was asked to ensure participant comprehension of each item's content.

[PAPER_0070, relevance_score=0.310] Following the in-lab visit, participants underwent the EMA portion of the study. In each of the EMA surveys, participants were asked how grateful they felt at the time of the prompt, whether they were engaged in capitalization at the time of the prompt, how close they felt with their most recent social interaction partner, and the timing of their most recent social interaction. Participants had a 15-min window to begin each survey, and if participants did not respond to the survey within 5 min, they received a reminder notification to complete the survey.

[PAPER_0053, relevance_score=0.316] Method

Transparency and Openness

This study's sample size, which included variables, hypotheses, and planned analyses, was preregistered on Open Science Framework in two separate registrations separated by the independent variable: daily capitalization (https://osf.io/3hdcz/) and active-constructive PRCA (https://osf.io/r9k4s/).

[PAPER_0059, relevance_score=0.300] Measures

Active-Constructive PRCA

The PRCA scale (Gable et al., 2004) assesses a capitalizer's perception of their close social partners' responses when they share positive events in their life. This 12-item scale is divided into four subscales of response types, each subscale consisting of three items. Active-constructive (α = .66) was the subscale of particular interest in the present study.

[PAPER_0061, relevance_score=0.223] Items for active-constructive include "They usually react to my good fortune enthusiastically," "I sometimes get the sense that they are even more happy and excited than I am," and "They often ask a lot of questions and show genuine concern about the event." Active-constructive PRCA was calculated by averaging the score of these three items.

[PAPER_0062, relevance_score=0.295] Momentary Gratitude

Momentary gratitude was measured during the EMA component of the study. At each survey prompt, participants were asked to report how much gratitude they were experiencing in the moment they received the survey notification. Responding to "I felt grateful," participants rated how grateful they felt on a 7-point scale from 1 (not at all) to 7 (extremely).

[PAPER_0067, relevance_score=0.302] Physical Health

The physical component score (α = .93) from the SF-36 Health Survey Version 2 (Ware et al., 2000) was used to measure physical health. Higher scores on the physical component indicates better health.

[PAPER_0074, relevance_score=0.263] The first set of MLMs assessed how capitalization attempts (separated into within- and between-person components) predict momentary gratitude, testing age, and social closeness (separated into within- and between-person components) as moderators of these effects. The second and third sets of MLMs assessed how trait-level active-constructive PRCA predicts momentary gratitude and capitalization.

Transparency and Openness

This study's sample size, which included variables, hypotheses, and planned analyses, was preregistered on Open Science Framework in two separate registrations separated by the independent variable: daily capitalization (https://osf.io/3hdcz/) and active-constructive PRCA (https://osf.io/r9k4s/).

[PAPER_0072, relevance_score=0.332] Analytic Plan

For the EMA variables, we calculated the person-mean for each individual by averaging their ratings across all prompts. Bivariate correlations were examined among active-constructive PRCA, age, frequency of momentary capitalization attempts (across all prompts), average momentary gratitude, average momentary closeness, physical health, and interaction recency. Correlations of the within-person variables were also assessed (see Table 2).

[PAPER_0073, relevance_score=0.415] Multilevel Modeling

We performed multilevel modeling (MLM) with prompts nested within person, included random slopes in all analyses and decomposed significant interactions using simple slopes (Aiken & West, 1991). We person-mean centered the within-person predictor variables and grand-mean centered the between-person predictor variables. Age was grand-mean centered. To examine effect sizes, we calculated semipartial R2 (Edwards et al., 2008).

[PAPER_0074, relevance_score=0.293] The first set of MLMs assessed how capitalization attempts (separated into within- and between-person components) predict momentary gratitude, testing age, and social closeness (separated into within- and between-person components) as moderators of these effects. The second and third sets of MLMs assessed how trait-level active-constructive PRCA predicts momentary gratitude and capitalization.

[PAPER_0075, relevance_score=0.383] Logistic MLMs were used when predicting momentary capitalization (a binary variable), including the models testing for age and both within- and between-person social closeness moderating the effects of active-constructive PRCA.

We conducted two types of robustness checks. First, we conducted an additional set of models controlling for social interaction recency. Social interaction recency was effect-coded such that having no social interaction within 30 min of the prompt was coded as -1 and having a social interaction within 30 min of the prompt was coded as +1.

[PAPER_0076, relevance_score=0.317] Then, this variable was person-mean centered to calculate the within-person component and grand-mean centered to calculate the between-person component. Second, physical health was added as a covariate in all models including age because a large body of research suggests negatively valenced affectivity is associated with poor physical health (e.g., Chida & Hamer, 2008; Pressman & Cohen, 2005). Results for all models were unchanged when controlling for the covariates interaction recency and physical health (see Tables S1-S4 in the online supplemental materials ).

[PAPER_0077, relevance_score=0.313] We ran secondary analyses to test the preregistered hypothesis examining the association between capitalization and closeness to replicate previous work. Controlling for age, people felt higher closeness on occasions where they capitalized compared to those where they did not capitalize. We further conducted exploratory analyses assessing lagged effects of gratitude. Controlling for gratitude at the previous prompt, all effects reported below hold in these models. Detailed results for these secondary and exploratory analyses are reported in Secondary Analysis, Exploratory Analysis, and Tables S5-S9 in the online supplemental materials .
